name: Whitening strips

image.caption: Plans to use Crest Whitening Strips

lead: Whitening strips are thin plastic films coated with peroxide gel that you press onto the front teeth for a set time each day. They are the most widely used consumer route to whiter teeth and give a brighter smile.

Hydrogen peroxide diffuses into the tooth and breaks apart pigment molecules from coffee, tea, wine and age, so the tooth reflects more light. Strips were introduced in the late 1980s, and randomized trials dating from 1992 have compared peroxide whiteners with placebo. A common protocol of twice daily for 30 minutes over 14 days is reported to lighten teeth by one or two shades.

paras: Users apply them for 30 minutes or so a day for one to several weeks, then repeat short touch-up courses as the colour fades. They are often the first whitening step before trays or dental treatment.

The main side effects are temporary tooth sensitivity and gum irritation, usually mild and fading after stopping. Strips cover mostly the front teeth and can fit unevenly on crowded teeth. Dental advice is commonly suggested before whitening over untreated decay or exposed roots.

angle.text: Users apply peroxide strips to lift stains and lighten tooth colour for a brighter smile, often as the first whitening step. The peroxide breaks down pigment in the tooth, and peroxide bleaching is well studied for whitening.

lead: Whitening strips are thin, flexible plastic films coated with a peroxide gel that are pressed onto the front surfaces of the teeth for a set period, typically daily over one to several weeks, to lighten tooth colour. They are sold over the counter and are among the most widely used consumer tooth-whitening products. [1][2]

They help people look better by lightening yellowing and staining on the visible teeth, which changes how a smile reads in photographs and in person. In looksmaxxing discussions, whitening is treated as one of the lowest-cost changes to the lower face, usually considered alongside orthodontics, veneers, dental cleaning and skincare. [3][4]

Peroxide bleaching works by delivering hydrogen peroxide (directly or from carbamide peroxide) that diffuses into the tooth and breaks down into reactive species that fragment pigment molecules, so that they reflect less colour. [1][5] Wikipedia reports that strips, introduced in the late 1980s, are typically applied twice daily for 30 minutes for 14 days and can lighten teeth by one or two shades within several days, depending on frequency of use and product. [1]

Reviews describe peroxide-based whitening as safe and effective when manufacturers' protocols are followed, with transient tooth sensitivity and gum irritation as the main side effects. [6][7] Randomized trials dating from 1992 have compared peroxide whiteners with placebo, and a 2020 meta-analysis of 20 trials compared strips with dentist-supervised bleaching. [8][9]
infobox: Late 1980s (home strips); Crest Whitestrips launched in 2001 [1][11]
Daily 30-minute applications over about 14 days, per product labels [1]
Lightens tooth colour by roughly 1 to 2 shades in typical use [1]
EU/UK retail products limited to 0.1% hydrogen peroxide; up to 6% under dental supervision [1][18]

paras: Strips are shaped to fit the buccal (outer) surfaces of the teeth, so they mostly cover the front teeth. [1] Related home options include paint-on whitening gels, tray-based carbamide peroxide systems worn for hours daily or overnight, whitening rinses and whitening toothpastes; the last use abrasives and sometimes low-concentration peroxide. [1] Dentist-supervised trays use higher peroxide concentrations, and in-office treatments use much higher concentrations with or without light activation. [1][2]

Wikipedia gives typical in-office gel strengths of roughly 10 to 44 percent carbamide peroxide, or about 3 to 16 percent hydrogen peroxide, with light-accelerated 'power bleaching' using 25 to 38 percent hydrogen peroxide. Carbamide peroxide became favoured in many products because it is more stable in storage than hydrogen peroxide. [1]

Some newer strips use other oxidising or whitening agents. A looksmax.org poster describes a strip product listing phthalimidoperoxycaproic acid (PAP) and bamboo charcoal instead of hydrogen peroxide. [10]

Efforts to whiten teeth are old. Wikipedia mentions ancient Roman use of urine with goat milk, oil pulling in Ayurvedic medicine, and barbers in the late 1600s filing teeth and applying acid. Oxalic acid and calcium hypochlorite were proposed in the 1870s, and in the 1940s and 1950s ether and hydrogen peroxide gels were used on living teeth. [1]

Dr William Klusmeier introduced custom-tray bleaching in the late 1960s, and a 1989 article by Haywood and Heymann supported the method; home plastic strips coated with peroxide gel followed in the late 1980s. [1] Procter and Gamble announced Crest Whitestrips in 2000 and introduced them in 2001, and later versions included the Supreme line (2003), Advanced Seal (2009), 3D models (2009 to 2011) and Supreme FlexFit (2013), according to Wikipedia. Its Supreme product contains 14 percent hydrogen peroxide and its Professional product 6.5 percent. [11]
Aesthetic dentistry has expanded considerably over the past century, with whitening now one of the most requested cosmetic dental procedures. [12][7]

Tooth whitening is a dynamic process involving diffusion of the whitening agent, interaction with stain molecules and micromorphological changes in the tooth. [5] Extrinsic stains arise from beverages, foods, tobacco and other environmental factors, and intrinsic discolouration from ageing, wear and developmental factors; bleaching mainly targets intrinsic and deeper stains that polishing cannot remove. [1]

Hydrogen peroxide produces reactive oxygen species that are linked in the literature both to the whitening effect and to sensitivity and gum irritation; Wikipedia notes that peroxyacid-based agents are described as producing fewer free radicals. [1] Tooth colour perception depends on lighting, background and surrounding tissue, and colour science underpins how shade is measured. [13]

A 1992 double-blind trial of two carbamide peroxide products reported whiter teeth than placebo after six weeks. [8] A 2007 randomized trial in 52 adults in Shanghai compared 6 percent hydrogen peroxide strips (Crest Whitestrips, twice daily for 7 days), a 5.9 percent paint-on gel and a water rinse. The strips produced the largest reductions in yellowness and the largest gains in lightness, and all three treatments were well tolerated. [14]

A 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials, with 20 trials after screening, compared strips with dentist-supervised bleaching. Supervised at-home bleaching produced a greater colour change on a spectrophotometer, with no significant difference on shade-guide scoring, and the authors state the instrumental difference was not visible to the unaided eye. Tooth sensitivity was lower with strips, and gum irritation and patient satisfaction did not differ significantly. Only two of the included trials were rated low risk of bias. [9] A 2018 Cochrane review has examined home-based chemical bleaching in adults. [15] A 2024 systematic review covers professional whitening. [16]

Wikipedia notes that much of the early lightening after intensive in-office whitening can rebound as teeth rehydrate, and that results fade gradually; people are advised in general guidance to avoid staining foods for the first 48 hours and may repeat treatment every six months to a year depending on habits. [1] Grokipedia states that 2 to 8 shade improvements are reported for extrinsic stains, with intrinsic stains such as tetracycline responding more slowly. [2]

Transient tooth sensitivity and gingival irritation are the most frequent side effects, usually resolving after stopping use. [6][7] Wikipedia reports sensitivity in 67 to 78 percent of people after in-office treatment with hydrogen peroxide and heat, and Grokipedia cites 8 to 66 percent of users across products. [1][2] The meta-analysis above found a lower risk of sensitivity with strips than with supervised at-home bleaching (risk ratio 0.78). [9]
Poorly fitting trays can cause gum irritation and chemical burns, and strips fit unevenly on crowded teeth, which can leave patchy coverage. [1]

A 2010 review by Goldberg and colleagues concluded that daily low-level whitening doses do not cause general toxicity, and that genotoxic and carcinogenic effects appear only at concentrations not reached in dental treatment. It lists local effects including pulp sensitivity, cervical resorption, changes to the enamel surface and release of components from restorative materials, and argues that decisions about whitening should rest with dental professionals. [17]

Wikipedia lists groups advised to use whitening with caution: people with peroxide allergy, sensitive teeth, cracks or exposed dentine, enamel defects, acid erosion, gum recession, active decay or defective restorations, and notes that pregnancy, breastfeeding and age under 16 are also listed. A prior oral examination is generally recommended. Whitening does not change the colour of existing crowns, veneers or white fillings. [1] The International Agency for Research on Cancer found insufficient evidence that hydrogen peroxide causes cancer in humans. [1]
Wikipedia also describes 'bleachorexia', an obsessive pattern of repeated whitening that resembles body dysmorphic disorder, and notes that over-bleaching can leave teeth looking translucent. [1]

In the EU and UK, retail whitening products are limited to 0.1 percent hydrogen peroxide, while dentists may use up to 6 percent and only dental professionals may apply it to patients aged 18 or older. [1][18] In the US, Wikipedia reports that the FDA is understood to accept gels up to 6 percent hydrogen peroxide or 16 percent carbamide peroxide, and that Brazil classifies whitening products as cosmetics. [1] The UK General Dental Council raised concerns in 2010 about untrained providers, and in a survey it ran, 83 percent of respondents supported regulation. [1]
Goldberg and colleagues have objected to peroxide products being sold as unrestricted cosmetics. [17] Market limits differ by country, so the products available at retail vary between markets. [18]

In January 2024 the AFP news agency reported warnings from French dental professionals, including David Couchat of the French Federation of Orthodontics, about at-home whitening strips, pens, gels, lamps and aligners promoted by influencers as a cheap, quick route to a better smile. The dentists said before-and-after images are often retouched and that many influencers have veneers covering their natural teeth. [18]

Teeth whitening is among the most commonly discussed low-cost appearance interventions in lifestyle communities, usually alongside veneers and orthodontics. T Nation threads mention whitening toothpaste and commercial strip products, and discussions of charcoal whitening have also appeared. [3][19]

On looksmax.org, threads include a question about whether whitening strips damage teeth [4], a thread asking about using strips during isotretinoin treatment [20], and a post about a charcoal-and-PAP strip product marketed through TikTok. [10]

Posters in these threads raise safety, sensitivity and effectiveness questions; dental literature describes beverages, foods and tobacco as main causes of extrinsic staining that whitening addresses. [1][20][4]

Products differ in peroxide type (hydrogen or carbamide peroxide), concentration, wear time, strip shape and coverage, and whether they carry professional-body endorsements; product labels give the manufacturer's regimen and contraindications. Wikipedia describes the Supreme product in the Crest line as the strongest and says it is also sold through dentists, and a 2009 Consumer Reports test ranked it first of eight products while noting it was also the most expensive. [11] Age guidance on the product line limits use for children under 12, and says Supreme is not recommended under 18. [11]

Professional cleaning removes extrinsic stains but not intrinsic ones; whitening toothpastes use abrasives and sometimes low-concentration peroxide; bonding and veneers can mask stains that whitening does not change. [1] A 2023 randomized trial compared a violet LED in-office system with other techniques, and a 2024 trial examined activated-charcoal products. [21][22]

The charcoal trial randomised 56 volunteers to charcoal powder, charcoal toothpaste, regular fluoride toothpaste or 10 percent carbamide peroxide for 14 days. Charcoal products produced whitening similar to regular toothpaste and carbamide peroxide produced the best whitening and satisfaction; the authors recommended discouraging charcoal products. [21]

Randomized trials show peroxide whiteners lighten teeth compared with placebo: a 1992 double-blind trial of two carbamide peroxide products reported significantly whiter teeth than placebo at six weeks [8], and a 2000 randomized controlled trial examined whitening efficacy and safety. [23] A 2007 trial compared strips, paint-on gel and a negative control. [14] A 2020 meta-analysis compared strips with supervised bleaching [9]; the 2018 Cochrane review covers home-based bleaching systems. [15] A 2024 randomized trial examined activated-charcoal products [21], and a 2023 trial compared violet-LED in-office whitening with other techniques. [22] A 2014 review summarised research as showing whitening to be safe and effective when manufacturer protocols are followed. [6]

lore.intro: Whitening strips appear on looksmax.org mainly in questions about safety and in product threads, and on T Nation in brief mentions of charcoal and whitening toothpaste. [4][10][3][19]

claims.claim: Whitening strips may damage teeth, so their safety is in doubt.
Using whitening strips during an isotretinoin (Accutane) course causes gum recession or discoloration.
Strips using PAP and charcoal instead of hydrogen peroxide whiten teeth effectively.
Charcoal toothpaste whitening does irreversible harm to teeth.
Strips are a cheap way to get visibly whiter teeth without a dentist.
Whitening results last only a short time and need repeating.
